title: Given daily prices, maximise profit from buying and selling a stock, covering the single-transaction case and the unlimited-transaction case. Explain both algorithms, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (Single and Multiple Transactions)

s1_definition.profdef: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock maximises trading profit from a price series. With a single allowed transaction we track the lowest price seen so far and the best profit of selling today at that minimum. With unlimited transactions the optimum is the sum of every positive day-over-day gain, which captures every upward move. Both run in a single linear pass.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India trading desk reviews a security's daily prices and wants the maximum profit, either from one clean buy-and-sell or from many back-to-back trades capturing every rise.
s1_definition.oneliner: One trade tracks the min and best sell; many trades sum every positive daily gain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock maximises trading profit from a price series. With a single allowed transaction we track the lowest price seen so far and the best profit of selling today at that minimum. With unlimited transactions the optimum is the sum of every positive day-over-day gain, which captures every upward move. Both run in a single linear pass.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India trading desk reviews a security's daily prices and wants the maximum profit, either from one clean buy-and-sell or from many back-to-back trades capturing every rise.

**One line to remember:** One trade tracks the min and best sell; many trades sum every positive daily gain.

sections.s2_technical:
For the single-transaction case we scan the prices, keeping the minimum price seen so far as the best buy point. On each day we compute the profit of selling that day, which is today's price minus the running minimum, and keep the best such profit. Because we only ever sell after buying, the running minimum guarantees the buy day precedes the sell day. For the unlimited-transaction case, the maximum profit is simply the sum of every positive difference between consecutive days, because capturing each individual upward step is equivalent to buying at every local trough and selling at every local peak.

The single-pass cores are `int minSoFar = prices[0], best = 0; for (int p : prices) { minSoFar = Math.min(minSoFar, p); best = Math.max(best, p - minSoFar); }` and `int profit = 0; for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) if (prices[i] > prices[i-1]) profit += prices[i] - prices[i-1];`. A concrete check: for prices 7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4 the single-transaction best is five, buying at one and selling at six, while the unlimited best is seven. Senior nuance: both are linear time and constant space; the bounded-k-transaction and with-cooldown variants need a small state-machine dynamic programming, but these two base cases are greedy and need no table.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India trading desk analyses a security's daily closing prices and wants the maximum profit achievable, both under a rule allowing just one buy-and-sell and under a rule allowing unlimited trades. Comparing every buy-sell pair is quadratic. This is exactly how Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock works: a running minimum solves the single trade, and summing positive daily gains solves unlimited trades.

The code defines a `StockTradingService` with `maxSingleTrade(prices)` and `maxUnlimitedTrades(prices)`. A `Demo` provides a price series and logs both profits.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is daily prices seven, one, five, three, six, four. Step 1 for the single trade: the running minimum starts at seven and the best profit at zero. Step 2: price one lowers the minimum to one. Step 3: price five gives a profit of four, which becomes the best. Step 4: price three gives profit two, no improvement; price six gives profit five, the new best; price four gives profit three, no improvement. So the single-trade best is five, buying at one and selling at six. Step 5 for unlimited trades: we sum each positive step, from one to five is plus four, from three to six is plus three, giving seven. We return single-trade five and unlimited seven.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
    │
    ├─ SINGLE TRADE ──────────────────┬─ UNLIMITED TRADES ──────────────
    │  minSoFar / best                 │  sum positive day-over-day gains
    │  7 → min7 best0                   │  1→5 : +4
    │  1 → min1 best0                   │  5→3 : skip
    │  5 → min1 best4                   │  3→6 : +3
    │  3 → min1 best4                   │  6→4 : skip
    │  6 → min1 best5  ◀ best           │  total = 7
    │  4 → min1 best5                   │
    ▼                                   ▼
  single = 5  (buy@1 sell@6)          unlimited = 7
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock is a family of problems, and I always separate the two base cases clearly. With a single allowed transaction, I scan the prices once while tracking the lowest price seen so far as my best possible buy point, and on each day I compute the profit of selling that day against that running minimum, keeping the best. Because the minimum only ever looks backward, the buy day is always before the sell day, so the answer is valid without comparing every pair.

With unlimited transactions, the optimum is simply the sum of every positive difference between consecutive days. Capturing each individual upward step is mathematically equivalent to buying at every local trough and selling at every local peak, so I just add up all the gains and ignore the drops. Both of these are greedy single passes in linear time and constant space with no table at all, which I contrast with the harder variants: limiting to at most k transactions or adding a cooldown day both require a small state-machine dynamic programming that tracks holding and not-holding states.

At the National Bank of India I used these on a trading desk to report the maximum achievable profit on a security's daily price series under different trading rules. I ran the running-minimum scan for the single-trade figure and the positive-gain sum for the unlimited figure, both fast enough for real-time dashboards. Explaining the running-minimum logic, why summing positive steps is optimal for unlimited trades, and how the k-transaction and cooldown variants escalate to a state machine is what shows an interviewer I understand this whole problem family.
